semantic_correction.stem: A nurse is teaching a client with asthma how to identify and reduce personal triggers. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Track whether symptoms worsen with allergens, respiratory infections, physical activity, smoke or poor air quality, then use the asthma action plan to reduce the triggers that apply to you.
options.B: Use the same trigger-avoidance plan as other people with asthma and reduce routine physical activity whenever symptoms occur, because trigger patterns are generally similar between clients.
options.C: Focus mainly on taking prescribed medicines, because environmental exposures and respiratory infections contribute little once long-term asthma treatment has been started.
options.D: Stay indoors and limit normal activity as the main prevention strategy, rather than tracking which allergens, infections, irritants, or activities actually worsen your symptoms.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current NHLBI guidance identifies indoor and outdoor allergens, respiratory infections, physical activity, and poor air quality or cold air as common asthma triggers. NHLBI also emphasizes that clients should identify their own triggers and incorporate trigger avoidance or reduction into an individualized asthma action plan; physical activity should not simply be avoided because treatment can allow most clients to remain active. B is incorrect because trigger patterns vary and blanket activity restriction is not recommended. C is incorrect because trigger management remains part of asthma control even when medication is prescribed. D is incorrect because broad inactivity or staying indoors is not a substitute for identifying the specific triggers that worsen the individual's asthma.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach clients with asthma to identify individualized triggers such as allergens, respiratory infections, physical activity, smoke or poor air quality and incorporate trigger reduction into an asthma action plan without unnecessary activity restriction.
semantic_correction.source_organization: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), National Institutes of Health

semantic_correction.source_locator: Asthma — Causes and Triggers → 'Asthma triggers': common triggers include indoor allergens, outdoor allergens, physical activity, infections such as colds/flu/COVID-19, and poor air quality or very cold air. Asthma — Managing Asthma → 'Know your asthma triggers': reduce exposure to identified allergens, air pollution, tobacco smoke, infection risks, and other personal triggers; physical activity should not simply be avoided and should be individualized with the provider. Asthma — Treatment and Action Plan → asthma action plan describes how to identify allergens or triggers to avoid and which actions or medicines to use when symptoms change.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: NHLBI identifies allergens, respiratory infections, physical activity, poor air quality and other irritant exposures as asthma triggers and supports individualized trigger identification and management as part of the asthma action plan.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests individualized asthma-trigger recognition and reduction with one clearly best answer and without absolute-word or obvious test-taking cues.

option_audit.A: Correct. Every trigger category and the individualized action-plan approach are directly supported by current NHLBI guidance.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Trigger patterns are individualized, and physical activity should not be broadly restricted simply because it can trigger symptoms in some clients.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Medication and trigger management are complementary components of asthma control; prescribed treatment does not make environmental or infectious triggers irrelevant.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Broad indoor confinement and activity restriction do not replace identifying and managing the client's actual trigger pattern.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone combines recognized trigger categories with individualized assessment and action-plan management; B assumes a universal pattern and promotes restriction, C dismisses triggers after treatment begins, and D substitutes nonspecific avoidance for individualized trigger identification.
cueing_check: All four choices are parallel asthma-management statements of comparable length and specificity; the prior repeated 'only' distractor pattern was removed and no option is structurally privileged by formatting.
